# Volume 5 — CHAPTER VIII. MISS WINIFRED INTERVENES

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

The following day, Miss Winifred paid a visit to the manse and interrogated Mary, who, as a youth possessing notable shrewdness and perception, recounted her experience in a straightforward and honest manner, completely devoid of swagger or grievances. Although Miss Winifred formed a more positive impression than she had anticipated, she considered it her obligation to maintain a stern demeanor.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0000 }

“Do you believe,” she asked in a stern tone, “that you displayed your thankfulness to this household, which has treated you with excessive kindness, when you insulted and pursued one of their small companions in the manner you did yesterday?”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0001 }

“Listen, I behaved in a terribly unkind way,” Mary readily confessed. “I have no idea what came over me. The old fool appeared to be such a convenient target. However, I felt deeply regretful—to be completely truthful, I wept over it in bed yesterday evening. Ask Ida if that isn’t true. I refused to inform her of the reason since I felt embarrassed, which led to her crying as well, out of fear that my feelings had been injured by someone. Goodness, I hardly possess any feelings that are worth mentioning. The thing that troubles me is the reason Mrs. Grimble hasn't come searching for me. That behavior is unusual for her.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0002 }

Although Miss Winifred found the situation somewhat strange, she simply gave Mary a stern warning against making any additional assumptions regarding the minister’s codfish, after which she departed to share the updates at Hollowmere.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0003 }

“Should the youngster's tale prove accurate, it is an issue that must be investigated,” declared she. “Trust me, I possess a bit of knowledge regarding that Grimble woman. Ambrose was once quite familiar with her during his time residing over-harbour. I recall listening to him remark last summer concerning her and an orphan under her care—in all probability this selfsame Mary-creature. He mentioned that an individual informed him she was pushing the youngster to the point of exhaustion while failing to properly feed and clothe her. You are aware, Nell dearie, that my rule has perpetually been to avoid interacting or interfering with those over-harbour people. However, I am going to dispatch Ambrose across the water tomorrow so he may ascertain the truth of the matter if possible. Following that, I will converse with the clergyman. Do not forget, Nell dearie, that the Ashdowns discovered this young girl in a state of actual starvation inside James Taylor’s former hay barn. She had remained in that place the entire night, frozen, famished, and solitary. Meanwhile, we were resting comfortably in our beds having eaten hearty evening meals.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0004 }

“The poor little thing,” Nell said, visualizing a cold, hungry, and solitary child like her own precious babies under those conditions. “Miss Winifred, if she has suffered ill-treatment, she cannot be returned to a place like that. I was formerly an orphan in an almost identical predicament.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0005 }

“The Hopetown asylum people will need to be consulted by us,” Miss Winifred said. “She cannot remain at the manse, regardless. Those poor children could acquire dear knows what from her. Swearing is something she has been known to do, as I understand. Just consider her staying there for two entire weeks without Mr Ashdown ever realizing it! A family is something a man of that sort has no business possessing. He should be a monk, why, Nell dearie.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0006 }

Miss Winifred returned to Hollowmere two nights afterward.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0007 }

“Nothing could be more astonishing!” declared she. “The exact morning following the flight of this Mary-creature, Mrs. Grimble was discovered deceased in her bed. For years her heart had been frail, and the physician had cautioned her that death could occur at any moment. Nobody was present in the home, since she had dismissed her hired laborer. The following day, certain neighbors discovered her body. It appears they noticed the child was missing, but they assumed Mrs. Grimble had dispatched her to her cousin close to Port Marlow, just as she had stated her intention to do. Because the cousin failed to attend the funeral, no one ever learned that Mary was not residing with her. Ambrose asserts that the individuals he conversed with recounted details regarding Mrs. Grimble’s treatment of this Mary that caused his blood to simmer. As you are aware, learning that a child has been mistreated throws Ambrose into an absolute rage. According to them, she thrashed her without pity for the slightest flaw or error. A few people spoke of contacting the asylum officials, yet what is everyone’s responsibility belongs to no one, and no action was ever taken.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0008 }

“I regret that the Grimble individual has died,” Tabitha declared vehemently. “It would please me to travel across the harbour to express my outrage to her. Denying a child food and striking them, my dear Mrs. Dr.! Naturally, I support proper disciplinary spanking, but nothing beyond that. Furthermore, what will happen to this unfortunate child at present, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr?”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0009 }

“I imagine we have no choice but to return her to Hopetown,” Miss Winifred remarked. “It seems to me that all the folks in this vicinity desiring a child from the home already possess one. Tomorrow I will consult with Mr. Ashdown and express my views regarding this entire matter.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0010 }

“And beyond a doubt she is going to, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha remarked, once Miss Winifred had left. “There is nothing she would hesitate to do, not even shingling the church spire if the notion struck her. Yet I am unable to comprehend how even Winifred Tolley is capable of speaking to a minister in that manner. A person would suppose he was merely an ordinary individual.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0011 }

Once Miss Winifred departed, Bess Carrow unbent herself out of the hammock in which she had been learning her lessons and stole off toward Fern Hollow. The rest had arrived beforehand. Kit and Tobias were pitching quoits using aged horseshoes obtained from the Glen blacksmith. Rupert was tracking ants upon a sunlit mound. Edmund, reclining on his belly amid the ferns, was reading out loud to Mary and Izzy and Grace and Ida out of an amazing volume of myths containing enchanting tales about Prester John and the Wandering Jew, dowsing rods and men with tails, about Schamir, the rock-splitting worm that unlocked the path to golden riches, about Fortunate Isles and swan-maidens. Discovering that William Tell and Gelert were likewise myths dealt a severe blow to Edmund; while he would lie awake the entire coming night because of the tale of Bishop Hatto; yet he cherished the legends of the Pied Piper and the San Greal above the rest. He recited them in a gripping manner, as the bells on the Tree Lovers chimed in the summer breeze and the chill of the twilight shadows drifted over the valley.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0012 }

“Tell me, aren’t those fascinating falsehoods?” expressed Mary appreciatively once Edmund was done reading the book.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0013 }

“Those are not untruths,” Izzy remarked with indignation.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0014 }

“Are you saying those are actually true?” Mary inquired with disbelief.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0015 }

“No—not quite. They resemble those spectral tales you tell. While they lacked truth—you never anticipated our belief in them, which meant they were not falsehoods.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0016 }

“The story regarding the divining rod isn't a lie, at any rate,” Mary said. “Old Jake Crawford from over-harbour is able to use it. People fetch him from all over whenever they need a well dug. Furthermore, I think I am acquainted with the Wandering Jew.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0017 }

“Oh, Mary,” Ida uttered, filled with awe.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0018 }

“I really do—as true as your being alive. A certain elderly man was at Mrs. Grimble’s on a single day during the previous autumn. He appeared sufficiently aged to be any age at all. She happened to be questioning him concerning cedar posts, inquiring whether he believed they would endure for long. And he replied, ‘Last well? They’ll last a thousand years. I know, for I’ve tried them twice.’ Well, if his age reached two thousand years, who else could he be except your Wandering Jew?”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0019 }

“I do not think the Wandering Jew would have anything to do with someone such as Mrs. Grimble,” Grace stated with conviction.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0020 }

“The tale of the Pied Piper is a favorite of mine,” Izzy remarked, “as well as mother's. My heart always aches for that unfortunate small lame boy who failed to stay abreast of the rest and was locked outside the mountain. His disappointment must have been immense. For the remainder of his days, I imagine he would spend his time pondering the marvelous spectacle he had lost out on and longing to have gained entry alongside the others.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0021 }

“However, his mother must have felt such joy,” Ida remarked in a low voice. “I believe the fact that he could not walk properly had grieved her for her entire life. She might have even wept over it at times. Yet she would not feel sorrowful any longer—not ever. His lameness would bring her happiness, as it prevented her from losing him.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0022 }

“One day,” Edmund uttered in a dreamy manner, gazing far off into the heavens, “the Pied Piper is going to arrive over that hill up there and travel down Fern Hollow, playing his pipe in a merry and sweet fashion. And I am going to pursue him—pursue him down to the coast—down to the ocean—far from all of you. I do not believe I will desire to depart—Kit is going to desire to depart—it is going to be quite an adventure—yet I will not. But I will be forced to—the melody is going to call and call and call to me to the point where I have to pursue.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0023 }

“We’ll all go,” exclaimed Izzy, becoming ignited by the spark of Edmund’s imagination, and nearly convinced that she was able to glimpse the derisive, receding outline of the mystical piper at the distant, shadowy extremity of the dale.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0024 }

“No. Here is where you will sit and wait,” Edmund declared, the unusual fascination radiating from his large, magnificent eyes. “You will await our return. Yet our coming back is uncertain—because so long as the Piper continues playing, we are unable to return. Around the globe he might pipe us. Even so, you will remain sitting right here, waiting—and waiting.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0025 }

“Oh, hush,” Mary said, trembling. “Edmund Carrow, stop looking like that. You make me uneasy. Are you trying to make me cry? I could easily picture that terrible old Piper walking off, with you boys going after him, while we girls stay behind here waiting by ourselves. I don't know the reason—I was never given to weeping—yet the moment you begin your talking, I am always brought to the verge of tears.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0026 }

Edmund beamed with a sense of victory. Exercising this influence over his associates—manipulating their emotions, stirring their anxieties, electrifying their spirits—brought him pleasure. It fed a certain theatrical impulse within his nature. Beneath his satisfaction, however, lay a strange, slight shiver of an inexplicable terror. The Pied Piper had felt remarkably genuine to him—just as though the swaying drape concealing what was to come had been briefly parted in the starlight-dappled twilight of Fern Hollow, bestowing upon him a faint vision of the future.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0027 }

Rupert, who approached their circle to deliver an account of the events occurring in the kingdom of ants, restored everyone to the world of reality.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0028 }

“Insects are awfully fascinating,” Mary cried out, pleased to get away from the gloomy Piper’s spell. “That mound in the cemetery was observed by Rupert and myself for the whole of Saturday afternoon. I had no idea insects possessed so much to them. Listen, but those tiny creatures sure are feisty—a few of them seem to launch an attack for no apparent cause, as far as we were able to tell. And a few of them lack any courage. Becoming so frightened, they merely curled themselves into a sphere and permitted the rest of the bugs to strike them. They refused to defend themselves whatsoever. A few of them show laziness and refuse to labor. Their loafing was witnessed by us. And a single ant perished from sorrow because a different ant was slain—refused to labor—refused to consume food—simply perished—that happened, truly to Go—oodness.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0029 }

A stunned hush hung over the room. That Mary had not intended to utter “goodness” was obvious to all. The looks Grace and Izzy traded would have been worthy of Miss Winifred herself. Rupert and Edmund appeared uneasy, while the lip of Ida quivered.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0030 }

Mary shifted in distress.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0031 }

“I didn't mean to let that escape—I really didn't, upon my—that is, as sure as you're alive, and I choked back part of it. It appears to me that you people in these parts are terribly easily offended. If only you could have listened to the Wileys during one of their arguments.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0032 }

“Ladies abstain from speaking in that manner,” Grace remarked, adopting an unusually proper tone.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0033 }

“It’s not right,” Ida murmured.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0034 }

“A lady I am not,” Mary stated. “What opportunity have I ever been given to be a lady? However, provided I can prevent it, I will not repeat that statement. My word on it to you.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0035 }

“Furthermore,” Ida remarked, “you cannot anticipate that your prayers will be answered by God if you use His name irreverently, Mary.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0036 }

“I don’t expect Him to answer them anyway,” declared Mary, who lacked faith. “For a week I’ve been requesting Him to resolve this Grimble matter, yet He hasn’t accomplished anything. I plan to quit.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0037 }

It was at this moment that Bess, out of breath, came.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0038 }

“Oh, Mary, I have information to give you. Mrs. Kerr was across the harbour and what do you suppose she discovered? Mrs. Grimble has passed away—her lifeless body was discovered in bed the day following your flight. Consequently, you will not ever need to return to her.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0039 }

“Dead!” Mary uttered, completely stunned. A shiver then passed through her.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0040 }

“Do you think my praying was involved in that somehow?” she begged Ida to answer. “If it was, I will not pray ever again for the rest of my life. Why, she could return and haunt me.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0041 }

“No, no, Mary,” Ida said in a comforting way, “it had not. Why, Mrs. Grimble’s death occurred long prior to your ever starting to pray concerning it whatsoever.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0042 }

“Indeed,” remarked Mary as she overcame her fright. “However, I must say it startled me. I would hate to imagine that my prayers caused someone's death. Her passing never entered my mind while I prayed. She did not appear to be someone on the verge of death. Was anything said about me by Mrs. Kerr?”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0043 }

“She mentioned that it was probable you would need to return to the asylum.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0044 }

“I suspected that,” Mary said despondently. “And after that they will assign me to another place—probably to a person who is exactly like Mrs. Grimble. Oh well, I guess I can endure it. I am strong.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0045 }

“I’m going to pray that you won’t have to go back,” Ida murmured under her breath, while she and Mary traveled on foot back to the manse.
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0046 }

“You may act however you wish,” Mary stated with conviction, “nevertheless I promise I will not. This prayer matter frightens me thoroughly. Look at the outcome. Had Mrs. Grimble passed away once I began to pray, my actions would have caused it.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0047 }

“Oh, no, it wouldn’t,” Ida said. “I wish I were able to explain things better—I know father could, Mary, if you’d talk to him.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0048 }

“Catch me! I do not understand your father at all, and that is all there is to it. In the middle of the day, he passes right by without noticing me. While I am not arrogant, I am not a door-mat, either!”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0049 }

“Oh, Mary, father simply acts like that. We are also invisible to him during the majority of the time. His mind is occupied with profound thoughts, nothing more. And my prayers will ask God to retain you in Seven Gulls—for the reason that you appeal to me, Mary.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0050 }

“Very well. Just do not allow me to learn about any additional folks perishing because of it,” Mary stated. “I would enjoy remaining in Seven Gulls very much. I am fond of it, as well as the harbour and the light house—plus you and the Carrows. You are my sole friends in my entire life, and departing from you would be terrible to me.”
{: #nw-v05-c08-p0051 }
